name: Aaron Sterling
sources: Sound on Sound — Inside Track: Morgan Wallen & Post Malone (https://www.soundonsound.com/techniques/inside-track-morgan-wallen-post-malone)
notes: The modern crossover session drummer, placed in PRODUCERS by the research as an instrumental-grammar entry. The entry calls one practice "the most engine-relevant fact in this file about loops versus players": "a co-producer built groove libraries derived from classic country records at various tempos, and the drummer then played fresh live performances, using the library only as a compositional reference. Model: reference groove informs the *pattern*, a human performance supplies the *timing and velocity*." That is exactly how this model is authored — a canonical, low-variance pattern (long fill grid, near-zero pattern switching, a single hat subdivision) carried by a played humanize with real jitter and a wide velocity spread. The grammar on that record is stated: "small dry kit, cross-stick verses, low fill density, 2&4 throughout, **no programmed layers**" — hence no clap layer, no snap lane and no `bass808` block, the last of which the entry states outright: "the album deliberately has no 808 sub, a reversal of the artist's pop practice." The band is documented too: "~74–100 straight on 2&4 on that record." ⚠ The entry states "Melody/chords: n/a"; what it does give is the room's personnel — "pedal steel (Paul Franklin), fiddle (Larry Franklin), acoustic and electric (Bryan Sutton, Derek Wells) and keys (Dave Cohen) — i.e. the classic live board." So **the melody, countermelody, chords and bassline numbers here are INFERRED** from that ensemble (steel and fiddle answering in the gaps, a warm open voicing, a plain root-motion bass) and none of them is a researched fact. ⚠ Confidence is medium (research: high-medium) — the loop-as-reference practice is directly documented, the rest is not.
